title: III. The Brothers Make Friends
paragraphs: Ivan wasn’t in a separate room after all. He was sitting in a corner closed off by a screen, where the other people in the room couldn’t see him. This was the first room inside the entrance, with a buffet along one wall, and waiters were constantly darting through it. The only customer was an old retired military man drinking tea in a corner. In the rest of the tavern, though, the usual racket went on: people shouting for waiters, corks popping, billiard balls clicking, the organ droning. Alyosha knew that Ivan didn’t normally come to this tavern and didn’t like taverns anyway. So, he reflected, Ivan must have come only to meet Dmitri, as they had agreed. But Dmitri wasn’t there.
“Shall I order you fish, or soup, or something? You can’t live on tea alone, I suppose,” cried Ivan, obviously delighted to have snapped up Alyosha. He had already finished dinner and was having tea.
“I’ll have soup, and tea afterwards. I’m hungry,” said Alyosha cheerfully.
“And cherry jam? They have it here. Remember how you adored cherry jam when you were small?”
“You remember that? Yes, I’ll have jam too. I like it still.”
Ivan signaled the waiter and ordered soup, jam and tea.

“I remember everything, Alyosha. I remember you up to the age of eleven, when I was nearly fifteen. Fifteen and eleven are so far apart that brothers can’t be companions at those ages. I’m not even sure I was fond of you. For my first few years away in Moscow I never thought of you at all. Then you came to Moscow yourself, and I think we met just once somewhere. Now I’ve been here over three months, and so far we’ve barely exchanged a word. I’m leaving tomorrow. I was sitting here just now, wondering how I could catch you to say good-by, and at that very moment you went by.”
“Did you want so much to see me, then?”

“Very much. I want to get to know you once and for all, and I want you to know me. Then I can say good-by. I believe it’s always best to get to know people right before you leave them. I’ve seen the way you’ve been watching me these three months. Your eyes have had a steady look of expectation, and I can’t bear that. That’s why I’ve kept my distance. But in the end I’ve come to respect you. The little man holds his ground, I thought. I’m laughing, but I mean it. You do hold your ground, don’t you? I like people who are firm like that, whatever it is they’re standing on, even small fry like you. Your expectant eyes stopped irritating me. I grew fond of them in the end, those expectant eyes. You seem to love me, for some reason, Alyosha?”

“I do love you, Ivan. Dmitri says of you—Ivan is a tomb! I say of you, Ivan is a riddle. You’re a riddle to me even now. But I’ve understood one thing about you, and I didn’t understand it until this morning.”
“What’s that?” laughed Ivan.
“You won’t be angry?” Alyosha laughed too.
“Well?”
“It’s that you’re exactly as young as other young men of twenty-three—a young, fresh, nice boy, green, in fact! There. Have I insulted you terribly?”

“On the contrary, it’s a coincidence that startles me,” cried Ivan, warmly and good-humoredly. “Believe it or not, ever since that scene with her I’ve been thinking of nothing but my youthful greenness, and then you start in on exactly that, as if you’d guessed. Do you know what I’ve been telling myself, sitting here? Say I didn’t believe in life. Say I’d lost faith in the woman I love and in the order of things, and was convinced that it’s all a disorderly, damnable, maybe devil-ridden chaos. Say I’d been hit by every horror of human disillusionment. I would still want to live. Once I’d tasted the cup, I wouldn’t turn away until I’d drained it! At thirty, though, I’m sure to put the cup down, even if I haven’t emptied it, and turn away—to where, I don’t know. But until thirty I know my youth will win out over everything, every disillusionment, every disgust with life. Many times I’ve asked myself whether any despair exists that could beat this frantic and perhaps unseemly thirst for life in me. I’ve decided that none does—until I’m thirty, that is; after that it will leave me by itself, I imagine. Some driveling, consumptive moralists, poets especially, often call that thirst for life low. It is a Karamazov trait, true enough, this thirst for life whatever happens. You have it too, no doubt. But why is it low? The centripetal force on our planet is still fearfully strong, Alyosha. I long for life, and I keep on living in spite of logic. I may not believe in the order of the universe, yet I love the sticky little leaves when they open in spring. I love the blue sky. I love certain people, whom one loves, you know, sometimes without knowing why. I love certain great deeds done by men, though I lost faith in them long ago, perhaps; but from old habit the heart still treasures them. Here, they’ve brought your soup. Eat it, it’ll do you good. It’s first-rate soup, they know how to make it here. I want to travel in Europe, Alyosha, and I’ll leave from here. And yet I know I’m going only to a graveyard—but what a precious graveyard! The dead who lie there are precious. Every stone over them tells of such burning life in the past, such passionate faith in their work, their truth, their struggle, their science, that I know I’ll fall to the ground, kiss those stones and weep over them. Though I’m convinced in my heart that it’s long been nothing but a graveyard. And I won’t weep out of despair. I’ll weep simply because my tears will make me happy; I’ll soak my soul in the feeling. I love the sticky leaves in spring, the blue sky—that’s all there is to it. It has nothing to do with intellect or logic. It’s loving with your insides, with your stomach. You love the first strength of your youth. Do you understand any of my tirade, Alyosha?” Ivan laughed suddenly.

“I understand only too well, Ivan. To love with your insides, with your stomach—that’s exactly what one longs for. You put it so well, and I’m awfully glad you have such a longing for life,” cried Alyosha. “I think everyone ought to love life above everything else in the world.”
“Love life more than the meaning of it?”

“Of course, love it regardless of logic, as you say. It has to be regardless of logic, and only then will you understand its meaning. I’ve thought so for a long time. Half your work is done, Ivan—you love life. Now you just have to try for the second half, and you’re saved.”
“You’re out to save me, but maybe I’m not lost! And what is your second half?”
“Why, that you have to raise your dead, who perhaps haven’t died after all. Come, let me have my tea. I’m so glad we’ve had this talk, Ivan.”
“You’re inspired, I see. I’m awfully fond of such _professions de foi_ from such—novices. You’re a steadfast person, Alexey. Is it true you mean to leave the monastery?”
“Yes. My elder is sending me out into the world.”

“Then we’ll meet again in the world. We’ll see each other before I’m thirty, when I start turning from the cup. Father doesn’t mean to turn from his cup until he’s seventy; he even dreams of clinging on to eighty, so he says. He means it only too seriously, buffoon though he is. He too stands on a firm rock: his sensuality—though after thirty, admittedly, there may be nothing else to stand on.... But clinging on to seventy is vile. Better to stop at thirty; one could keep ‘a shadow of nobility’ by fooling oneself. Have you seen Dmitri today?”
“No, but I saw Smerdyakov,” and Alyosha gave a quick but detailed account of meeting Smerdyakov. Ivan listened anxiously and asked him questions.
“But he begged me not to tell Dmitri that he’d told me about him,” Alyosha added. Ivan frowned and thought it over.
“Is it on Smerdyakov’s account that you’re frowning?” asked Alyosha.
“Yes, it’s because of him. Damn him, I really did want to see Dmitri, but now there’s no point,” Ivan said reluctantly.
“But are you really leaving so soon, brother?”
“Yes.”
“And Dmitri and father? How is it going to end?” Alyosha asked anxiously.

“You keep harping on that! What’s it got to do with me? Am I my brother Dmitri’s keeper?” Ivan snapped irritably, then suddenly smiled bitterly. “That was Cain’s answer about his murdered brother, wasn’t it? Maybe that’s just what you’re thinking? Well, damn it all, I can’t stay on here as their keeper, can I? I’ve done what I had to do, and I’m going. Do you think I’m jealous of Dmitri, that for three months I’ve been trying to steal his beautiful Katerina Ivanovna? Nonsense. I had business of my own. I’ve finished it. I’m going. I finished it just now, and you were there to see.”
“At Katerina Ivanovna’s?”

“Yes, and I’ve freed myself once and for all. And anyway, what has Dmitri got to do with me? He doesn’t come into it. I had my own business to settle with Katerina Ivanovna. You know, in fact, that Dmitri acted as though we had some understanding. I didn’t ask him to. He solemnly handed her over to me and gave us his blessing. It’s all too funny. Ah, Alyosha, if you knew how light my heart is now! Believe it or not, I sat here over my dinner and almost ordered champagne to celebrate my first hour of freedom. Tfoo! It dragged on for nearly six months, and all of a sudden I’ve shaken it off. Even yesterday I couldn’t have imagined how easy it would be to end it, if I chose.”
“It’s your love you’re speaking of, Ivan?”

“Call it my love, if you like. I fell in love with the young lady. I tormented myself over her, and she tormented me. I sat keeping watch over her ... and suddenly it’s all collapsed! This morning I spoke with inspiration, and then I went off and roared with laughter. Can you believe it? Yes, it’s the literal truth.”
“You seem very cheerful about it now,” Alyosha remarked, looking at his face, which had suddenly turned brighter.

“But how was I to know I didn’t care for her at all! Ha ha! Apparently I didn’t. And yet how she drew me! How attractive she was just now, when I made my speech! And do you know, she draws me terribly even now, and still it’s so easy to leave her. Do you think I’m boasting?”
“No. It’s only that perhaps it wasn’t love.”

“Alyosha,” laughed Ivan, “don’t philosophize about love; it doesn’t suit you. The way you plunged into the argument this morning! I forgot to kiss you for it.... But how she tormented me! It really was like sitting next to a ‘laceration.’ Ah, she knew how I loved her! She loved me, not Dmitri,” Ivan insisted gayly. “Her feeling for Dmitri was just self-laceration. Everything I told her just now was perfectly true. The worst of it is that it may take her fifteen or twenty years to see that she doesn’t care for Dmitri and loves me, the one she torments. She may never see it at all, in spite of today’s lesson. Well, it’s better so; I can simply leave for good. By the way, how is she now? What happened after I walked out?”
Alyosha told him she had been hysterical, and that now, he’d heard, she lay unconscious and delirious.
“Isn’t Madame Hohlakov laying it on?”
“I don’t think so.”
“I’ll find out. Nobody dies of hysterics, anyway. They’re nothing. God gave women hysterics as a relief. I won’t go to her at all. Why shove myself forward again?”
“But you told her she never cared for you.”
“I did it deliberately. Alyosha, shall I send for champagne? Let’s drink to my freedom. Ah, if you only knew how glad I am!”
“No, brother, we’d better not drink,” said Alyosha suddenly. “Besides, I feel somehow low.”
“Yes, you’ve been low for a long time; I’ve noticed.”
“So you’ve made up your mind to go tomorrow morning?”

“Morning? I never said morning.... Though it may turn out to be the morning. Believe it or not, I came to dine here today only so as not to dine with the old man, I loathe him so. As far as he’s concerned, I’d have gone long ago. But why does my leaving worry you so? We have plenty of time before I go—an eternity!”
“If you’re leaving tomorrow, how can you talk of an eternity?”

“What difference does it make to us?” Ivan laughed. “We have time enough for our talk, for what brought us here. Why do you look so surprised? Tell me: why did we meet here? To talk of my love for Katerina Ivanovna? Of the old man and Dmitri? Of travel abroad? Of the fatal position of Russia? Of the Emperor Napoleon? Is that it?”
“No.”

“Then you know what for. Other people may differ, but we, in our green youth, have to settle the eternal questions before anything else. That’s what we care about. Young Russia talks of nothing but the eternal questions right now, just when the old folks are all taken up with practical ones. Why have you been watching me expectantly for the past three months? To ask me, ‘What do you believe, or don’t you believe anything at all?’ That’s what your eyes have been saying all this time, isn’t it?”
“Maybe,” Alyosha smiled. “You’re not laughing at me now, are you, Ivan?”

“Me, laughing! I don’t want to hurt my little brother, who’s watched me so expectantly for three months. Alyosha, look me straight in the face! Of course I’m just the same sort of little boy you are, only not a novice. And what have Russian boys been up to until now—some of them, I mean? Take this stinking tavern, for instance. They meet here and settle in a corner. They’ve never met before in their lives, and when they walk out of the tavern they won’t meet again for forty years. And what do they talk about in that brief stop at the tavern? About the eternal questions: whether God exists, and immortality. And those who don’t believe in God talk about socialism or anarchism, about remaking all humanity on a new pattern, which comes to the same thing, since they’re the same questions turned inside out. And masses, masses of the most original Russian boys do nothing but talk about the eternal questions! Isn’t it so?”

“Yes. For real Russians the questions of whether God exists and of immortality—or, as you say, the same questions turned inside out—naturally come first and foremost, and so they should,” said Alyosha, still watching his brother with the same gentle, inquiring smile.

“Well, Alyosha, it’s sometimes very unwise to be a Russian at all, but you can hardly imagine anything stupider than how Russian boys spend their time. Still, there’s one Russian boy named Alyosha that I’m awfully fond of.”
“How nicely you slipped that in!” Alyosha suddenly laughed.
“Well, tell me where to start; give your orders. The existence of God, eh?”
“Start wherever you like. Yesterday at father’s you declared there was no God.” Alyosha searched his brother’s face.

“I said so at dinner yesterday on purpose, to tease you, and I saw your eyes light up. But now I have no objection to discussing it with you, and I say that in all seriousness. I want to be friends with you, Alyosha, since I have no friends and want to try it. Well, just imagine, perhaps I accept God too,” Ivan laughed; “that surprises you, doesn’t it?”
“Yes, of course, if you’re not joking.”

“Joking? Yesterday at the elder’s they told me I was joking. You know, dear boy, in the eighteenth century there was an old sinner who declared that if there were no God, He would have to be invented. _S’il n’existait pas Dieu, il faudrait l’inventer._ And man really has invented God. What is strange, what would be marvelous, is not that God actually exists. The marvel is that the idea of the necessity of God could get into the head of a creature as savage and vicious as man. It is so holy, so touching, so wise, and it does such credit to man. As for me, I made up my mind long ago not to ask whether man created God or God created man. I will not run through all the axioms Russian boys have laid down on that subject, every one of them derived from European hypotheses. What is a hypothesis there is an axiom to the Russian boy—and not just to the boys but to their teachers as well, since our Russian professors are often the same boys themselves. So I skip all the hypotheses. What are we after now? I am trying to explain, as quickly as I can, my essential nature: what sort of man I am, what I believe in, and what I hope for. That is it, isn’t it? And so I tell you that I simply accept God. But note this: if God exists, and if He really created the world, then, as we all know, He created it according to the geometry of Euclid, and He made the human mind able to conceive only three dimensions of space. Yet there have been, and still are, geometers and philosophers, some of them among the most distinguished, who doubt whether the whole universe—or, to put it more broadly, the whole of being—was created only according to Euclid’s geometry. They even dare to dream that two parallel lines, which by Euclid can never meet on earth, may meet somewhere in infinity. I have concluded that if I cannot understand even that, I cannot expect to understand anything about God. I admit humbly that I have no faculty for settling such questions. My mind is Euclidian and earthly, so how could I solve problems that are not of this world? And I advise you, my dear Alyosha, never to think about them either, above all about God, whether He exists or not. Such questions are wholly unsuited to a mind created with the idea of only three dimensions. So I accept God, and gladly. More than that, I accept His wisdom and His purpose, which are utterly beyond our understanding. I believe in the underlying order and the meaning of life. I believe in the eternal harmony into which, they say, we will one day be blended. I believe in the Word toward Which the universe is striving, Which Itself was ‘with God,’ and Which Itself is God, and so on and so on, to infinity. There are all sorts of phrases for it. I seem to be on the right road, don’t I? And yet, believe it or not, in the end I do not accept this world of God’s. Though I know it exists, I do not accept it at all. You must understand, it is not that I do not accept God; it is the world He created that I do not and cannot accept. Let me put it plainly. Like a child, I believe that suffering will be healed and made good, that the whole humiliating absurdity of human contradictions will vanish like a pitiful mirage, like the despicable invention of the feeble, infinitely small Euclidian mind of man. I believe that in the world’s finale, at the moment of eternal harmony, something so precious will happen that it will be enough for every heart, to comfort every resentment, to atone for all the crimes of humanity and for all the blood they have shed. I believe it will make it possible not only to forgive but to justify everything that has happened to men. But even if all that comes to pass, I do not accept it. I will not accept it. Even if parallel lines do meet and I see it with my own eyes, I will see it and say that they have met, and still I will not accept it. That is the root of me, Alyosha; that is my creed. I mean what I say. I began our talk as stupidly as I could, deliberately, but I have led up to my confession, because that is all you want. You did not want to hear about God; you only wanted to know what the brother you love lives by. And so I have told you.”
Ivan finished his long tirade with striking and unexpected feeling.
“And why did you start ‘as stupidly as you could’?” asked Alyosha, regarding him with a dreamy look.

“First, to be Russian about it. Russian conversations on such subjects are always conducted unbelievably stupidly. And second, the stupider you are, the nearer you are to reality. The stupider you are, the clearer you are. Stupidity is short and plain, while intelligence squirms and hides. Intelligence is a rogue, but stupidity is honest and direct. I’ve steered the conversation toward my despair, and the more stupidly I’ve put it, the better for me.”
“And will you explain why you won’t accept the world?” said Alyosha.

“Of course I will, it’s no secret; that’s what I’ve been leading up to. Dear little brother, I don’t want to corrupt you or shove you out of your stronghold. Perhaps I want you to heal me.” Ivan suddenly smiled just like a gentle little child. Alyosha had never seen such a smile on his face.
